results.title: Why Humans Still Matter in the Age of Intelligent Machines
results.author: Jonny Caplan
results.content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
Key Takeaways
- ChatGPT said:
AI shouldn’t replace human creativity, it should amplify it by handling information, research and execution while humans provide instinct and purpose.
- Human experience, irrational confidence and the ability to care deeply about an idea are qualities AI cannot truly replicate.
There is a lot of talk at the moment about what AI is going to replace, and I find the whole conversation slightly backward because we seem obsessed with asking what AI can do that humans currently do, rather than asking what it can never really do and why those differences are actually what could make the relationship between humans and AI so powerful.
For all the extraordinary things AI can do, there are some things it simply cannot replicate in the way a human being experiences them. It can analyze emotion, understand language, recognize patterns and produce something that sounds incredibly sensitive, but it doesn’t actually feel anything. It doesn’t know what it is like to walk into a room and instantly sense that something is wrong before anybody has said a word, or to meet somebody for five minutes and have an inexplicable feeling that you should trust them, or perhaps that you absolutely shouldn’t.
It can understand the language of emotion, but there is a very important difference between understanding an emotion and actually having one.
The same applies to instinct, which I think is one of the most underrated qualities in entrepreneurship. Some of the biggest decisions people make are not based entirely on data, because sometimes you look at something and you simply know that it is right, even though you cannot necessarily explain why.
You cannot always put instinct into a spreadsheet or build a model around it, because instinct is often the accumulated result of everything you have experienced, every mistake you have made, every success you have had, every person you have met and every lesson you have learned, including many of the lessons you didn’t even realize you were learning at the time.
AI doesn’t have that life experience. It has information, an almost absurd amount of information, and it can process that information at a speed and scale that is extraordinary, but it hasn’t actually lived any of it. It hasn’t made a terrible decision at 28 and spent the next ten years remembering exactly why it was terrible.
It hasn’t walked into a meeting completely unprepared and somehow managed to turn it into the best deal of its career.
It hasn’t had somebody tell it that an idea is impossible and then become slightly obsessed with proving them wrong, partly because it believes in the idea and partly because it now really wants to prove that person wrong.
I don’t want AI to be me
All that is exactly why I think AI can be such an extraordinary assistant.
I don’t want it to be me. I want it to be the perfect counterpart to me because the very things that make AI different from us are precisely what make it so useful. I want something sitting there that doesn’t get tired, doesn’t need a coffee, doesn’t have to go home, doesn’t get offended when I say, “No, that’s rubbish, start again,” and doesn’t start wondering whether I have any idea what I am actually doing. I want to be able to throw an idea at it at midnight, completely change my mind twelve minutes later, ask it to approach the whole thing from another direction, decide that direction is terrible, go back to the original idea and then suddenly come up with something completely different, and have it still sitting there ready to help.
It doesn’t moan, it doesn’t sulk, it doesn’t complain that we’ve already done three versions, it doesn’t need a weekend, it doesn’t need a holiday and it doesn’t decide that because somebody else got the better project, it is going to quietly resent me for the next six months. It doesn’t need feeding, it doesn’t need sleeping and, importantly, it doesn’t cheat.
Well, not very often.
AI is occasionally an idiot
It is also, occasionally, an absolute idiot, which I actually find quite reassuring.
You can have a brilliant conversation with AI, get to a genuinely interesting thought, and then suddenly it will confidently tell you something that is completely wrong, misunderstand something you’ve explained three times or produce something that is technically perfect but has absolutely no idea why anybody should care about it. The funny thing is, this makes it considerably more human than some people who are currently predicting the end of humanity, because humans get things spectacularly wrong, too.
The difference is that humans can have a terrible idea and then, five minutes later, have a brilliant one. We can become irrationally passionate about something that nobody else understands, we can take a risk when all the available evidence tells us not to, and we can sometimes be arrogant enough to believe that we can do something everybody else thinks is ridiculous. That arrogance, in the right person and in the right circumstances, can be an incredibly powerful thing because, without a certain amount of irrational confidence, a huge number of businesses, inventions, films, products and ideas would probably never have existed.
And there is some pretty compelling evidence suggesting we are not talking about a distant future here. Stanford’s 2025 AI Index found that 78% of organizations surveyed reported using AI in 2024, up from 55% in 2023, while the proportion using generative AI in at least one business function more than doubled, from 33% to 71%. McKinsey’s research has also found that 64% of respondents say AI is enabling innovation in their organizations, although only 39% report an impact on EBIT at the enterprise level. I think this is an important distinction, because adopting AI and actually knowing how to use it properly are clearly two very different things.
That is the bit I don’t want us to lose.
I don’t want a future where humans start trying to think like machines simply because machines are better at processing information. I want the opposite. I want a future where humans can become even more human because machines take care of more of the things they’re good at.
Steve Jobs put it rather brilliantly when he said, “Technology is nothing. What’s important is that you have a faith in people,” arguing that if you give smart people good tools, they can do wonderful things with them. That was said in 1994, long before anybody was talking about ChatGPT or generative AI, but I actually think it is one of the most relevant observations you can make about where we are heading now, because the technology may be extraordinary, but it is still the person using the technology who decides what is worth creating.
Let’s let humans decide
Let AI do the research. Let it organize the information, find the patterns, challenge the thinking, generate the alternatives, and help turn an idea into something tangible much faster than we could have done before, but let the human decide whether any of it is actually worth doing.
Because creativity isn’t simply the ability to produce ideas. It is the ability to care about an idea enough to pursue it when other people don’t understand it, to recognize something special when it appears in front of you and, perhaps most importantly, to have the courage to back yourself when there isn’t enough evidence yet to prove that you are right.
AI can give you a thousand possibilities, but somebody still has to choose one. It can analyze the market, but somebody still has to walk into the room. It can write the pitch, but somebody still has to stand there and believe in it. It can tell you what the data says, but there will always be moments when an entrepreneur looks at the data and says, “I know what it says, but I don’t believe it.”
And sometimes that person will be completely wrong. But sometimes they will be right, and those are the moments that change everything.
That is why I don’t see AI as the end of human creativity. I see it as potentially the greatest creative partner humans have ever had, because for the first time we can have something sitting alongside us that can absorb an extraordinary amount of information, work at extraordinary speed, never get tired and never get bored, while the human being remains responsible for the things that make the work worth doing in the first place.
The human brings the soul, the instinct, the emotion, the ambition, the experience, the irrational confidence, the humour and, occasionally, the stupidity. AI brings the patience, the memory, the processing power, the research, the speed and the extraordinary willingness to have another go without ever saying, “For God’s sake, we’ve been through this already.”
And maybe that is actually the perfect relationship.
One of us needs sleep, and one of us doesn’t. One of us occasionally has absolutely no idea what we’re doing, and the other one can produce a remarkably convincing answer even when it has absolutely no idea what it is doing either. One of us has instincts, emotions, and a lifetime of experiences that cannot be reduced to data, while the other has access to an enormous amount of knowledge and can help turn those instincts into something real.
That sounds less like a battle between humans and AI to me and much more like the beginning of a very happy marriage.
Provided, of course, the human remembers who is supposed to be in charge.
Key Takeaways
- ChatGPT said:
AI shouldn’t replace human creativity, it should amplify it by handling information, research and execution while humans provide instinct and purpose.
- Human experience, irrational confidence and the ability to care deeply about an idea are qualities AI cannot truly replicate.
There is a lot of talk at the moment about what AI is going to replace, and I find the whole conversation slightly backward because we seem obsessed with asking what AI can do that humans currently do, rather than asking what it can never really do and why those differences are actually what could make the relationship between humans and AI so powerful.
For all the extraordinary things AI can do, there are some things it simply cannot replicate in the way a human being experiences them. It can analyze emotion, understand language, recognize patterns and produce something that sounds incredibly sensitive, but it doesn’t actually feel anything. It doesn’t know what it is like to walk into a room and instantly sense that something is wrong before anybody has said a word, or to meet somebody for five minutes and have an inexplicable feeling that you should trust them, or perhaps that you absolutely shouldn’t.
It can understand the language of emotion, but there is a very important difference between understanding an emotion and actually having one.
results.summary:
Artificial intelligence should function as a powerful creative partner that amplifies human potential by handling data-heavy tasks while leaving instinct, purpose, and final decision-making to human entrepreneurs.

### Key Points
- Stanford’s 2025 AI Index reports that 78% of organizations used AI in 2024, a significant increase from 55% in 2023.
- McKinsey research indicates that while 64% of organizations use AI for innovation, only 39% report a measurable impact on enterprise-level EBIT.
- AI excels at processing information, recognizing patterns, and maintaining tireless execution, but it lacks genuine human emotion, life experience, and intuition.
- Human qualities like irrational confidence and the ability to care deeply about an idea remain essential for driving business innovation and creative breakthroughs.
- The most effective use of technology involves humans retaining control to determine which ideas are worth pursuing, rather than relying on machines for strategic judgment.

### Why it Matters
The integration of AI into business workflows is rapidly accelerating, yet many organizations struggle to translate these tools into tangible financial results. By positioning AI as a supportive counterpart rather than a replacement, leaders can leverage machine efficiency to enhance the unique, irreplaceable human instincts that drive true innovation.

results.title: Harvey Smith Explains What Most Games Are Missing And Why He’s Still Making Them: ‘It’s An Act Of Rebellion To Try To Do Something Hopeful In Times Like This’
results.author: John Walker
results.content:
Last month, Dishonored co-creator Harvey Smith and Arkane’s former production director Ben Horne announced that they had established a new studio, Black Pony Immersive, with the sole purpose of creating a new immersive sim in the lineage of Deus Ex, Thief, Prey, and System Shock. Insistent on learning more about how the studio came to be and its ambitions for the future, we sat down with Smith and Horne to talk about defying the odds in a precarious gaming industry, the rebellious act of developing in a genre that publishers are afraid to touch, and the deliciousness of mystery. Oh, and what it’s like when you have a limited budget for chairs.
When Arkane Austin was closed by Microsoft in 2024, Harvey Smith and Ben Horne were both beyond devastated. But even among the carnage and sadness, they knew what they were going to do next. Both were of a single mind. In the aftermath of the awful news, Horne came to Smith and said, “You know what we should do?”
“I think I’m going to complete your sentence for you,” Smith replied at the time. “What if we start a studio?”
It wouldn’t be until a year later that Black Pony Immersive was officially formed, and then another year before the studio was unveiled to the public. So what took place in that first year?
“Just talking to every person that we thought might be able to fund us,” says Harvey Smith. “You talk to VCs and they start talking about NFTs or AI, and we’re like, ‘Guys, best of luck.’ You talk to some and they’re like, ‘No, no, we’re not into that at all. We like what you’re about, the fundamentals of your game, but our people are hoping to see, uh, times one thousand return within two years.’”
“You hear a lot of ‘no’s from people,” adds Horne. People asked them, are you guys leveraging any bleeding-edge technology? Or, are we going to get a return on investment super-quickly? “It really sharpened our focus around who are the right partners for us. Not just, ‘how can we get off the ground as quickly as possible?’, which in our hearts is what we wanted to do. We just burned to make this thing, to make this kind of game with these people. But we learned so much about what really matters to us, what we’re willing to accept.”
Eventually, something (and we don’t know what) worked out, leading to Black Pony Immersive receiving enough funding to establish a 26-person studio. “Pretty much no-strings-attached,” adds Smith. “We’re just doing what we think is right every day.”
Of course, this is a far tighter budget than either had been used to after many years as a subsidiary of Bethesda, which is owned by Microsoft. “The downside is you don’t have endless money,” explains Smith. “If you need more money or more people or better chairs, you can’t just snap your fingers and do that. We don’t have any of that, we’re fully remote.” Smith then gestures to the lack of any furniture beneath him. “Uh, I’m standing up.”
“We’re a scrappy little team,” Smith continues, “and we hope to pull off what Looking Glass did, or what Origin did, or what Ion Storm did, or what Arkane and Raphael [Colantonio] certainly did.”
But isn’t there a kind of hubris to this? How many developers have created their own AA team and set out to make the sorts of games they’ve previously achieved under AAA publishers and come up short? “I think my nature…we’re kind of humble,” says Smith in response. “I’ve failed hard a couple of times. Maybe three, depending on how you count it. And it teaches you more than success. Everybody calling you brilliant and loving your shit doesn’t really teach you anything, other than it feels good to be called brilliant.” But then, perhaps there needs to be some boldness too, Smith says. “I don’t want to call it arrogance,” he adds, “but it’s not fair to call it confidence. I’m not the most confident person. It’s some sort of defiance. It’s an act of rebellion to try to do something hopeful in times like this.”
A guiding spirit
There was something unexpectedly poignant about the announcement of Black Pony Immersive. The date of the reveal was planned long in advance, but what no one expected was that the day before, Warren Spector would announce his retirement. Spector, seen by many as the father of the immersive sim genre, has been a close friend and mentor of Harvey Smith’s ever since the latter’s first job as lead tester on System Shock. The pair went on to work together for nine years. The two announcements back to back was, I commented, like a death and a birth.
“I have all these incredible texts back and forth from Warren,” says Smith, immediately emotional. “We’re going to lunch soon to talk about all this, but we did not coordinate this. God, I have such weird feelings about this, because on one hand, well deserved! And watching the whole industry go through turmoil is so hard on the soul, right? Trying to go to bat over and over and having a tidal wave hit you is very difficult. But, at the same time, it’s sad too, because you want to see people keep doing what they do well forever. He’s amazing.”
“And the guy’s 70,” I interject. “True,” says Smith. “I never could have asked for a more patient, exuberant mentor. And I learned so much. I’m eternally thankful to Warren.”
When the Heart speaks
One of Harvey Smith’s driving passions is to create games that stay with players long after they’ve finished them, games that “get into their fucking heads, and they talk about for 10, 20 years, and you can see the delight, the cartharis. I have so many letters, I save all those…we had a fucking wedding.”
A wedding?
“For Dishonored. These two amazing people wanted to get married, someone reached out and said they want to theme it all Dishonored, it’s all going to be in costumes.”
The PR team in London told Smith about this and asked if he’d write a few lines for the Heart. Something for the couple to have read out at their wedding. The Heart was one of the most fascinating parts of Dishonored, a literal heart, once belonging to Jessamine Kaldwin, that you could hold and that would offer poetic insights into the NPCs in the game’s world, a wholly optional feature that gave the setting of Dunwall so much more color.
Smith continues, “I sat down and immediately wrote a bunch of lines from the perspective of the Heart. I texted April Stewart who did the voice for Jessamine and the Heart [and also plays Cartman’s mom on South Park] and I explained what was happening. She was like, ‘Oh my God, I’m gonna go to the kitchen right now, my partner and I are going to record these lines on my iPhone.’”
It didn’t stop there. “I went to Thomas Mitton and said, ‘Hey dude, we’ve gotta do some more Heart lines.’ He’s like, ‘But we’re not working on a project!’ [I said] ‘I know, I know, but check it out!’”
Mitton was also immediately on board. “So all the reverb and wind sounds and the heart beating and the echoing voice and all that shit, he recorded them, and so we sent them to the PR team, and they were like, ‘What the fuck?!’”
At the wedding, one member of the couple held up a Dishonored Heart that someone had made, and they played the lines over the speakers. The lines were written from the perspective of one person analyzing the other person to see if they were the right match.”
All the way through this anecdote, Ben Horne was audibly gasping, sitting more and more upright in his chair as the tale went on. Even he’d never heard about this before. Smith explains, “There’s more lucrative stuff to do, there’s saner stuff, and there’s stuff that hurts less when it goes bad. But the reason you do it—cynical people call it parasocial, but it’s this connection with the audience, and if you’re a musician or a writer or a filmmaker, a video game maker—if you know you know. It’s very powerful because you’re not doing this shit for yourself. Nobody’s writing a novel and then pitching it into the fucking fireplace. It’s so hard to write a book, and it’s so hard to make a game. So you’re doing it for this connection between humans.”
Embracing the mystery
Black Pony Immersive is not ready to talk about the game it’s working on, but I wanted to get an idea of why it’s working on one. What is the ambition behind the project?
“You know, the longer you’re in games,” Smith muses, “the more you see the same model play out over and over. And then somebody suddenly does something that feels fresh. Like [2021’s creepy deckbuilder] Inscryption, it had a sense of mystery in it, and I so rarely see mystery in games. Real mystery. Games are about systems and UI and pointers to the player, and helping the player understand what’s happening in this weird tech that you’re interacting with, right? So technology works against mystery. And Inscryption came out, and it had this feeling of mystery that I loved so much; it was delicious.”
Around the same time, Smith points out, Elden Ring also came out. “I had bounced off all the Souls games, but in Elden Ring you just wander around Limgrave and you hear that music, and you’re just constantly possessed with ‘what is around the corner?’” He tails off for a moment, and then reminds himself he can’t get into any specifics. “Doing something that is magical like that, that even if you’ve played games for 30, 40, 50 years, it feels novel in some way, it feels special, it feels like someone loved this and gave it their all, it feels like it has a voice, people still talk about it in 10 years. That would make me feel successful.”
Smith remembers sitting next to the FTL designers at an awards show, and wanting to spend the entire evening telling them not just why he loved their game, but stories from it, anecdotes about specific adventures.
He then recalls a line from Doug Church, the project lead on System Shock, who said, “When a game really works, people get together later and tell stories as if it actually happened. As if they played football, or went to war, together.”
Smith says this is what he wants from his game. “That joy, that magic between people.”
results.summary:
Dishonored co-creator Harvey Smith and former Arkane director Ben Horne have launched Black Pony Immersive, a new independent studio dedicated to developing original immersive simulation video games.

### Key Points
- Black Pony Immersive is a 26-person, fully remote studio founded by Harvey Smith and Ben Horne following the 2024 closure of Arkane Austin.
- The founders secured independent, no-strings-attached funding after rejecting venture capital offers that prioritized rapid returns or specific technology trends like AI and NFTs.
- The studio aims to create immersive sims in the tradition of genre-defining titles such as *Deus Ex*, *Thief*, *Prey*, and *System Shock*.
- Smith and Horne are prioritizing creative freedom and long-term player connection over the high-budget, high-pressure constraints of AAA publishing.
- The studio’s development philosophy focuses on fostering mystery and player-driven storytelling, drawing inspiration from titles like *Inscryption* and *Elden Ring*.

### Why it Matters
The formation of Black Pony Immersive represents a significant pushback against the industry trend of consolidating talent into massive, risk-averse AAA studios. By operating as a small, independent team, the founders are attempting to preserve the niche immersive sim genre while proving that creative, player-focused experiences can thrive outside of traditional corporate structures.

results.title: Dropbox breach seemingly caused by egregious authentication failure [U]
results.author: Ben Lovejoy
results.content:
Multiple Dropbox users have been emailed by the cloud storage company to advise them that a security breach saw unauthorised access to their account. Update: the company has said that about 5,000 accounts were compromised, with files downloaded from around 1,500 of them.
The root cause appears to be a lack of authentication by Dropbox when attackers created a single sign-on option through a third-party company …
Developer Yoni Levy posted a copy of the email he received on X.
We are writing to let you know that we’ve observed unauthorized access to your Dropbox account between August 4 and August 21, 2026. While our logs show no evidence that your files were viewed or downloaded, we want to share with you what happened, what we are doing about it, and what additional steps you can take.
Other Dropbox users reported receiving the same email in which the company said it resulted from a problem with a single sign-on (SSO) option using Lenovo IDs.
Dropbox partners with Lenovo as an identity provider so that users can log in to their Dropbox accounts using verified Lenovo IDs. While you may not have an existing Lenovo ID, our investigation determined that an issue with Lenovo’s email verification process allowed an unauthorized party to register a Lenovo ID using your email address and then use that Lenovo ID to log into the Dropbox account associated with that email address.
However, while Dropbox claims the flaw was in Lenovo’s email verification process, the bigger issue appears to be that Dropbox itself did not require users to use their existing login to verify the new SSO, as The CyberSec Guru reports.
- Recon/selection: The attacker compiles target email addresses (breach corpora, LinkedIn, customer lists — email addresses are effectively public data).
- Rogue IdP enrollment: The attacker registers a Lenovo ID as victim@example.com . No inbox access is needed because Lenovo’s verification step is missing or bypassable. The display name is set to something disposable — one victim who reclaimed the rogue account found the name “John Madden,” the late NFL broadcaster, a strong tell of bulk, low-effort registration.
- Federated sign-in: The attacker clicks “Continue with Lenovo” on Dropbox. Lenovo’s authorization server issues a token whose email claim matches the victim’s Dropbox account.
- Implicit account linking: Dropbox resolves the email claim to the existing account and mints a session. No password prompt, no step-up, no “link this new identity?” consent. From Dropbox’s perspective, a trusted IdP had already vouched for the address.
9to5Mac’s Take
While there was certainly a failure to verify email addresses at the Lenovo end, it would not have done any harm if Dropbox had authenticated the linked ID before it could be used to sign in. Failing to do so is an egregious fault.
The company has now fixed the flaw and expired all sessions previously ‘authenticated’ through a Lenovo ID.
If you don’t already have two-factor authentication enabled for Dropbox, it is highly recommended to change this immediately.
Photo by Shubham Dhage on Unsplash
results.summary:
Dropbox has confirmed a security breach affecting approximately 5,000 user accounts, caused by a flaw in the single sign-on integration process between the cloud provider and Lenovo.

### Key Points
- Unauthorized access occurred between August 4 and August 21, 2026, with files downloaded from roughly 1,500 accounts.
- The vulnerability stemmed from a Lenovo email verification process that allowed attackers to register accounts using victims' email addresses.
- Dropbox failed to require secondary authentication or user consent when linking new Lenovo IDs to existing Dropbox accounts.
- The company has since patched the security flaw and terminated all active sessions authenticated through the compromised Lenovo ID integration.
- Users are strongly encouraged to enable two-factor authentication to protect their accounts from future unauthorized access attempts.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the significant security risks associated with federated identity systems when platforms fail to implement rigorous account-linking protocols. It serves as a critical reminder for users to maintain multi-factor authentication, as even trusted third-party integrations can become vectors for unauthorized data access.

results.title: Now Hear This: September 2026
results.author: Ron Hart
results.content:
Now Hear This is a monthly A&R column that provides you with exciting new sounds we discovered through the innovative new music discovery platform Groover.
Each month, you can expect a varied bouillabaisse of songs from a vast spectrum of artists from all over the globe, regardless of genre or geography.
For September, SPIN has selected 21 artists who deserve your attention, including the Southern barstool groove of The Jardani Crow Band, the Gothic Americana of Until They Burn Me, the gnashing alt-metal of Kutie, the THX dreampop of Landroid, the late-night synthpop of Sonic Anonymous, the uplifting classic house of Chris Giuliano, the quiet folk of Gordon Shirley III, the American trapwave of GODHOUSESTARS, the poetic indie rock of Purse Thief, the psychedelic Atlanta hip-hop of The Difference Machine, the rap activism of No Face Lonewolf and The Illumin8tives, the California Britpop of The Mar Mars, the Motorik-paced big rock of The Train Rockers, the desert AOR of FireBug, the experimental “goo-core” of Shmu, the early ’00s NYC indie rock of Red Parks, the folk-and-reggae-tinged indie rock of Portland Oregon’s Harpool, the excitable emo pop of Lost in the City, the full-throttle desert rock of Paul Dunne, the feral power pop of Loose Buttons and the ska-punk heartbreak of Darby31.
Who knows, your next favorite act could just be a read away.
Jardani Crow Band
Sounds like: A jolt of Asheville bar band electricity coursing through a New Orleans groove that creates a feel reminiscent of The Wallflowers and Counting Crows.
Interview:
Describe your approach to music and how you would explain your sound to others.
MIKE– Besides wearing the Indie Folk/Americana/Roots Rock Vibe on my sleeve along with a good dose of post punk grit and raw story telling influences, I think that major thing is my non-traditional singing voice paired with these extremely beautiful and different female background vocals.
“I feel that one of the main strings/threads to all of these songs is the incredible background singers! One of the things that made these recordings so special is that each vocalist brought their own unique style, approach, and personality to the music, adding something truly distinctive to every track. Rather than simply having them sing solely predetermined parts, I encouraged each singer to contribute their own ideas and creative interpretation. A great example is the modulation section towards the end of Heart Attack song. The last thing we recorded was the pedal steel on this song, and the Pedal steel player is Bryan Daste, our co-producer, and he used Clare’s background as the sounding board for his playing! I told Clare that the breakdown section was completely hers to shape as she saw fit, almost like a solo feature. She responded by creating an incredible three-part harmony that added so much depth and emotion to the song. and like i said..helped shape the pedal steel playing. I took a similar collaborative approach throughout the project, allowing each musician the freedom to bring their own voice and artistry to the recordings.
The vocalists are featured as follows:
• Clare Dove (UK) – Fairytale of New Orleans, Rappaccini’s Daughter, Heart Attack, Love Section, Come What May
• Dorothy Takev (Bulgaria) – Midnight Moon, Train, Pathway to Hell
• Ally Rozario (Malaysia, via Belarus) – Her Song, Sand & Broken Shells
• Amanda Williamson (New Orleans) – Midnight Moon, Sand & Broken Shells & Love Section
Each of these artists contributed something unique, and their individual talents helped shape the character and feel of the songs in remarkable ways.”
Rip – Our main difference is we start off with an idea and with each artist we encourage them to express with free range adding their personal flavor to the song and we contribute ideas to fit more into what we hear, and the result is a magical transition into the final mix.
How did you come up with the name of your act?
Mike : Having reconnected with my oldest friend Rip on Bass, we have played in 3 other bands together and have done 4 other full length original albums. We were looking for a name together and over the course of texting back and forth ideas. Rip was telling me of his emotional and spiritual connection with his friends and family in Section, Jamaica and how we walked the trails of the John Crow Mountains. We wanted to honor that feel and use that as our cornerstone/sounding stone for our band. So we came up with “The Jardani Crow Band” –note Jardani means:
Jardani (Slavic) – ‘to be strong’; Jardani (Albanian) – ‘of the earth’ . But it’s an alternative to John…Rip has this great picture of him and his wife in front of the sign….That’s the inspiration.
Rip – We have a home in Section Portland Jamaica and that region is called The John Crow Mountains, so we found the word Jardani which is associated with John the Baptist and the apostle John, we knew Jardani Crow Band was a perfect fit for this project.
What are some artists and albums that have informed your creative direction?
Mike– Wilco meets Big Star meets Tom Petty meets The Replacements is a good start. The albums that I love are: all 3 Big Star Albums, Wilco: a.m and Yankee Hotel Foxtrot(we heavily used Impossible Germany for the vibe for Heart Attack…I doubled my acoustic and I doubled my electric guitar part and paired with Bryan Daste’s(our co-producer and engineer) amazing Pedal steel work I think we captured that type of vibe and sound. The Tom Petty album that I always come back to are: Damn the Torpedos, Long After Dark, and Hard Promises. and for the Replacements: “Tim”, “Let it Be”, and I still have a very used cassette tape of Hootenanny somewhere!
Rip – My early days of absorbing new bands was captured by The Clash, Chicago, Sex Pistols, Bob Marley, Wilco, Grateful Dead and early R.E.M. and more but these were my top influencers.
What’s the most exciting thing happening in music right now?
Mike – Well for us it’s being able to connect with these amazing musicians worldwide and to bypass the machine of major record labels to have 100% control of our vision and what we are doing. Obviously, there is a lot wrong out there, with the loss of kids joining bands and more focused on songwriters and people who are blessed by their family connections and don’t pay dues or even understand what dues are. Right? Technology like the use of SessionWire and Mixup(not paid sponsor) allows us to work remotely with our Producer in Portland, Rip in New Orleans and Me in Asheville, NC to all be on the same DAW and have these killer remote sessions. The same with these amazing sessions we have with musicians all over the world: France, UK, Croatia, Brazil, Japan,Malaysia, Canada, South Korea, and USA.
Rip – I agree with Mike, the advancements of technology and software gives us the ability to work with musicians from around the globe while working in real time.
Where do you see the music world heading in the next five years?
Mike – I hope the young musicians find their unique voices and learn to love creating music with their peers. That collective bonding is what grows your soul and adds beauty to your journey. Billy Strings, Jessie Welles, Amyl and the Sniffers, Wetleg and Wolf Alice are all killing it. IMHO.
Rip – That’s a loaded question because for me I see the music world in 5 years leaning more to AI and less work from the artist to achieve songs that normally would take musicians weeks and months to create. We’er working to preserve the art of writing songs with human heart and mind.
Mike: I hope we are showing how making music is done right and also how rewarding it can be.
How is music helping you during these uncertain times?
Mike – Music saves me from too much thinking and too much drinking. But seriously, Whenever I am down or feeling out of sorts I always force myself to write something new and I push myself. It always makes me feel better in the creation of a new song or riff that NEVER would have existed if I wasn’t in that state of mind. On a side note, during the COVID shut down, to 100% sound hyperbolic, Phoebe Bridges and her music saved me…. She was there with me during the shutdown-..she was putting out her content of playing songs live in her room and the honesty, her incredible voice, and songwriting skills inspired me when i needed it most. I have been told my approach to songwriting and style and the way I do passing notes in chords, use weird tunings, lyrics approach is similar to her. I was honored in that comparison. To show the influence for the track “Pathway to hell” during the last verse: we took the mix and sent it through a bus and left out my lead vocals and drums only….to create my voice on top of this sonic low fi vibe that Phoebe does in many of her songs.I love the way it came out.
Rip – Creating music has always been a relief from the chaotic world we live in from day to day. My brain is constantly creating riffs, hooks, melodies, lyrics, rhythms and ideas for new songs. I’ve been operating this way all of my life so now it’s a part of my daily life without the pressure for new material. Music definitely helps keep me grounded. And through our music we are able to meet people like yourself with positive vibrations.
Until They Burn Me
Sounds like: An arresting combination of Goth rock and Americana that comes across like a supergroup featuring members of Faith No More and 16 Horsepower.
Interview:
Describe your approach to music and how you would
explain your sound to others.
We approach our music very simply: we write what we want to hear. We are not at all concerned with the “correct” way to write a song. Which is a good thing, because neither of us have ever received any musical training, so we wouldn’t know how to do it anyway. We’ve never been concerned with choosing a style either. We just seemed to end up being a kind of rock/alt/country/Americana/punk/folk outfit with a splash of southern gothic, a sprig of voodoo and a dark temperament.
How did you come up with the name of your act?
The name came from lyrics written by Travis Martin 35 years ago when we were in our former band, The Dry Season. It’s a song called ‘Walking My Realms’, and the line was, “so in my walk I turn to shadow, I’ll ride the wind, Until They Burn Me“. It was kind of a way to honor and remember where we came from. While we wanted to do some new things and take our music in different directions than we had thus far done, I think it was important to stay connected to that lineage.
What are some artists and albums that have informed your
creative direction?
The first Mr. Bungle album was life-changing for all of us. The intentional chaos, musicianship, and energy was unlike anything we’d ever heard before. Or since, really. It was a gorgeous and terrible nightmare! Additionally, I would say Tom Waits, Bauhaus, The Stooges and Pink Floyd would probably be our biggest influences.
What’s the most exciting thing happening in music right
Now?
The rapidly uprising resistance to AI slop is probably the most exciting thing happening right now. And certainly the most important thing happening right now. We wear our flaws, rough edges, and imperfections like a badge of honor. For us, music is all about the feel. The raw grit and texture of underproduced music has always been a very effective sound for us. That’s the good stuff. It’s what allows people to empathize with each other. To communicate and share all of the experiences of life. And that just can’t be replicated artificially. Viva humanity! Viva Heathens!
Where do you see the music world heading in the next five years?
Things change so fast that it is very difficult to try to predict even five years in the future. But we would love to see the decline of corporate AI “music” and the exploitation of artists by streaming platforms. We would love to see music return to the days when it was exciting. Grass roots. Made with passion and originality. Physical media. We would love to see the return of vinyl and cassettes and CDs. The whole experience of music the way it used to be. Back in the good old days. Most young people these days have never experienced music this way and it’s a real shame.
How is music helping you during these uncertain times?
Are these uncertain times? I’m not so sure… Well, anyway, music is giving two old men something constructive to do instead of chasing them punk kids off our lawns and bitching about the price of gas. (Over $5 a gallon in Washington! Can you believe that?)
Kutie
Sounds like: Alt-metal alchemy from Clovis, California, that splits the difference between Paramore and Bloodlet.
Interview:
LANDROID
Sounds like: Star Wars-inspired (check the THX-1138 synthline!), endlessly romantic spin on fuzzed-out dreampop crafted in the California desert.
Interview:
Describe your approach to music and how you would explain your sound to others.
We usually describe our music as cinematic synthpop. There’s definitely some shoegaze and dreampop in there, some electronic music, and a little bit of a noir quality too.
We think a lot about atmosphere and how a song makes you feel. We love creating music that feels beautiful but also a little strange or unsettling, like there’s something happening beneath the surface that you can’t quite put your finger on.
Someone once described our music as the soundtrack to driving through the desert at night, and I thought that was pretty accurate.
How did you come up with the name of your act?
I’d been looking for a good band name my entire life. It’s surprisingly hard to find one that doesn’t suck.
When Greg and I moved out to the desert from Los Angeles, we ended up in Landers, California. One day we were at Pappy & Harriet’s, the big music venue out here, and I was talking to Linda Krantz, who was one of the owners at the time. I told her we lived in Landers and she said, “Oh, you live in Landers? You’re Landroids.”
And I immediately thought, “Oh my God. That’s the band name I’ve been looking for my whole life.”
I turned to Greg and said, “That’s our band name. We’re LANDROID.”
And that was it. We’ve been LANDROID ever since.
We pull inspiration from all over the place. David Lynch and the world of Twin Peaks have probably influenced us as much as any musician has. We love that combination of beauty, mystery, darkness, humor, and things that feel surreal.
What are some artists and albums that have informed your creative direction?
Musically for me, Beach House and the Cocteau Twins are big influences. Bloom and Heaven or Las Vegas are both perfect records, in my opinion. Greg loves Pink Floyd, Stevie Wonder, and John Coltrane (Elvin Jones is his drumming hero). Dark Side of the Moon? I mean, come on. It’s another perfect album. It might be the ultimate perfect album. And A Love Supreme. Does it get better than that? And then Nigel brings his love for artists like Radiohead, Bright Eyes, and Bon Iver and voilà! You have LANDROID. It’s a mish mash, for sure. We’re dreamy, but we’re also rock’n’roll.
What’s the most exciting thing happening in music right now?
I think one of the most exciting things happening in music right now is that, even with the rise of AI, there seems to be this opposite reaction where people are really valuing things that feel tangible and human. We’ve seen that firsthand. We sell a surprising number of CDs (who knew people even had CD players anymore?!), vinyl records, cassette tapes, and other physical things.
It feels like people are placing more value on actually being in a room together and experiencing music in real time through live performances, too. I love that. The more technology becomes part of our lives, the more people seem to crave connection and things they can hold with their hands. That’s exciting.
Where do you see the music world heading in the next five years?
I think AI is obviously going to change music in ways that none of us completely understand yet. I wish AI would clean my house or do my laundry and not try to write songs or create art, but it’s happening, and I don’t know that it can be stopped.
There’s going to be an enormous amount of music being created, and I think it’s going to become more difficult to know what’s real, who made something, and maybe even what “making music” means.
But I also think that’s going to make the human part of music more significant. People are going to want to know the story behind the songs and feel connected to the people making the music. Live shows, physical releases, and communities built around artists are going to become increasingly important. That’s where I hope it goes, anyway.
How is music helping you during these uncertain times?
Music is really how Greg, Nigel, and I process life. Sometimes we don’t even know how we feel about something until we’ve written a song about it. There’s something about taking whatever you’re carrying around, consciously or unconsciously, and turning it into music that can be incredibly healing.
And music does something to us physically and mentally, too. Whether you’re bouncing around at a show, standing there listening and feeling the frequencies, or just being in a room full of people experiencing the same thing together, something shifts in you and it’s usually for the better. That feels vital right now. We spend so much of our lives separated from each other behind screens. Music brings us back into our bodies and back into community. There’s an ancient need to gather together around music and have a collective transcendent experience. It’s our church, for sure.
Sonic Anonymous
Sounds like: “Weird, existential, late-night synthpop for the burnt-out generation” that sounds like a homespun take on Tame Impala.
Interview:
Describe your approach to music and how you would explain your sound to others.
When I was 8, I found an Elvis record in the basement and knew I wanted to perform music. A year later I heard Bob Dylan and realized I needed to write it too. I think there’s a real relationship between a song, the writer, and the instrument. I tend to play used gear because every instrument already has a story, and I invite it to sit down and have a chat. From there it usually lets me share mine, and the whole thing becomes this stream-of-consciousness way of processing whatever we’re carrying. Music is one of the few places I don’t have to perform a version of myself for anyone else… but, if I’m being honest, I do hope other people connect with it, too.
How did you come up with the name of your act?
It comes from a pretty personal place. I spent a lot of years masking, basically trying to be whatever version of myself I thought I was supposed to be. “Sonic” is about having something to say. “Anonymous” is about the fact that it could be me, you, or anyone carrying similar emotions. Framing it that way lets me make the project less about me specifically and think about the shared emotions a lot of people carry. The deadpan guy in the bathrobe with the flashing “JOLLY” tiara is the visual for a forced smile, the mask, while feeling drained behind closed doors. It’s ultimately about acknowledging the hard stuff, growing through it and still showing up.
What are some artists and albums that have informed your creative direction?
My influences are all over the place. I keep coming back to Neil Young’s “ditch era,” Bowie, Zappa, Phish, Can and Talking Heads — those completely changed how I think about music.
Funny enough, most of my demos start out sounding like outtakes from The Kinks’ Low Budget, I also have a real appreciation for French pop — both Gainsbourgs, Juniore, and pretty much anything bossa nova. I have to mention Keren Ann. In 2010, I wrote her a letter telling her how much her albums meant to me and she actually wrote back. It was specific and kind. She even listened to one of my songs and said it wasn’t really her thing, but she loved the piano… that sticks with me to this day.
Recent heavy rotation includes Anna Erhard, Dry Cleaning, Aldous Harding, Cate Le Bon’s Pompeii, St. Vincent’s Daddy’s Home, Deradoorian’s Ready for Heaven (that bass and percussion synchronization is incredible), Automatic, Reggi Roomers, Godley & Creme, and 10cc.
What’s the most exciting thing happening in music right now?
The amount of access we have now. Anyone can write, record, and put something out at a high level without waiting for permission. You can test ideas, work with great session players remotely, and just keep refining until it feels right. That freedom still blows my mind.
At the same time, people seem to be getting tired of only writing in their rooms and wanting to get back out. Musical collaboration is electrifying when you can bring different perspectives and levels of talent together in one room. And if you’re worried there’s no place to play, go support your local open mics – it fosters the musical ecosystem.
Where do you see the music world heading in the next five years?
AI is the obvious one. Everyone’s talking about it, and I think it’s going to create a split in how people listen. Some will lean into AI-generated music the same way people got into HDR photography or anime… one doesn’t replace the other, it just opens another lane with its own fans if it’s properly disclosed as AI content.
The models are getting better, but it’s also more predictable, and people are getting better at spotting it. I think that will push a group of listeners toward human-made music and an interest in album releases instead of just 30 seconds of social media hooks. We’ll probably see more AI-fronted acts, AI labels, even holographic pop stars that tour like an EDM show. There needs to be real regulation. Tech companies are already paying voice actors to train AI models, and that same approach should be applied to music. Instead of scraping an independent artist’s catalog for free, gain the artist’s consent and pay royalties rather than just taking the data.
At the end of the day, listeners, fans, and artists have to take action and support music in ways that signal to the industry that money can still be made through touring and album-based releases. So go to shows, listen to full records, buy physical merch, read tastemaker blogs. Otherwise, people are just complaining while consuming what’s on the menu and quietly normalizing the things they claim to oppose.
How is music helping you during these uncertain times?
Music is one of the few things that still cuts through the noise. It’s a universal language. You can put musicians from completely different backgrounds in a room, people who don’t even speak the same language, and someone starts on a note, and everyone just knows what to do. Suddenly there’s a shared moment that didn’t need words. That’s beautiful and it builds community through something as simple as sound and feeling.
Chris Giuliano
Sounds like: Uplifting, classic house that definitely has all the hallmarks of summertime on the dancefloor with its progressive fervor and crisp piano undercurrent.

How did you come up with the name of your act?
Simple. It’s just my name. No frills!
What are some artists and albums that have informed your creative direction?
Above & Beyond’s Tristate album was an important record for me. I also became heavily influenced by the sound design coming out of drum & bass and dubstep in the late 2000s. I’m always keen on and working towards unique sound design, and that’s become a pretty big part of how I approach production.
What’s the most exciting thing happening in music right now?

Where do you see the music world heading in the next five years?

How is music helping you during these uncertain times?
Music has always been a complement to life for me, and it’s also a mindful-release during difficult times. It’s one of the few things that can soothe your emotional state. Gordon Shirley III
Sounds like: Quiet, intricate folk from somewhere in Georgia imbued by slide guitar reminiscent of Chris Whitley.
Interview:
Describe your approach to music and how you would explain your sound to others.
My approach to music is very simple and very solitary. All songs feel different when they start to surface. Some come hard and fast, like you’re riding a wave and holding on for dear life, trying not to lose your grip. Others are like a long‑distance call — a feeling that the universe is ringing and you don’t know how to answer. It rings so quietly you’re not even sure you hear it, and you strain to listen past the noise. If you’re lucky enough and quiet enough, sometimes the call comes through.
I’m not a product or a project. I’m just a real, imperfect guy with a box of broken crayons trying to paint the best picture I can. My sound leans toward quiet, character‑driven folk with a little Southern melancholy. I grew up around a lot of talented musicians in Georgia, and that storytelling tradition stayed with me. The songs are simple, usually just guitar and voice, and I try to let the lyrics carry the weight.
Even when I use modern tools to help create a nice recording, the heart of what I do is still very human — one person, one guitar, and whatever feeling I’m trying to conjure in that moment.
How did you come up with the name of your act?
The name of my act is just my name. I use Gordon Shirley III because I grew up in a house with three Gordons — my grandfather, my father, and me. My grandfather was simply called Pa, my dad went by Junior, and I was given a very typical Southern nickname: Doodle.
So when it came time to share music, I figured Gordon Shirley III sounded a whole lot better than Doodle. It also felt honest. It’s who I am, and it carries the history of the family I grew up in — three generations of Gordons, all different and all the same.
What are some artists and albums that have informed your creative direction?
I’ve always been drawn to artists who write with honesty and a little bit of vulnerability — people who sound like they’re telling you the truth, even when the story gets messy. Loudon Wainwright III was one of the first songwriters who made me realize you could be funny, sad, and painfully honest all in the same breath. Blaze Foley showed me how fragile a song can be and still hit like a hammer.
And even though I may not sound like Cat Stevens, Nick Drake, or Jim Croce, little pieces of them show up in unexpected places — a turn of phrase, a quiet moment, a certain way a guitar line leans. They were part of the soundtrack of my life, and some of that inevitably finds its way into the songs.
I grew up listening to all kinds of music, but those artists and albums gave me permission to write the way I naturally do: simple, human, a little worn around the edges, and focused on the story more than the shine. I’m not technical at all — I mostly feel my way around, and try to trust where I’m going.
What’s the most exciting thing happening in music right now?
I think one of the most exciting things happening in music right now is watching artists like Stephen Wilson Jr. break through. He’s doing something raw and emotional that feels both familiar and brand new, and it reminds me that there are still people out there writing from the gut.
But honestly, the biggest change — and the most beautiful one — is what’s happening because of TikTok. For the first time, so many wonderful, talented musicians who used to only play for their family on the couch, or hide away in their basement making songs that would never see the light of day, are getting some well‑deserved attention.
I’ve always believed that musical gifts are far more common than people think. There are thousands of folks out there with voices, stories, and melodies that could stop you in your tracks — they just never had a way to be heard. Now they do, and watching those quiet, hidden artists suddenly find an audience feels like one of the most hopeful things in music.
Where do you see the music world heading in the next five years?
I think the music world is heading toward something more open and a lot less gatekept. Music can be whatever it needs to be for you. I think there will always be plenty of opinions about it, but not many rules.
Electronic tools and software have been part of music for decades — long before AI showed up — and they’ve shaped everything from home recording to the way people write. AI is more complicated, of course. I’d like to think of it as just another tool, but I know it isn’t that simple. It’s here, and it’s not going away. Is it evil or a blessing? Like everything else, it’s probably both.
What matters to me is that the heart of music still comes from people. Whether someone is writing on a guitar, producing on a laptop, or using new technology to help shape a sound, the feeling behind it is what makes it real. I think the next five years will be a mix of old and new — more voices, more ways to create, and fewer barriers keeping people from sharing what they make.
How is music helping you during these uncertain times?
Music helps me every day, whether I am struggling to make a song or listening to it cranked up in my car. Music lets me time‑travel to the special moments in my life. As I get older, it’s become great therapy for me.
For so many years, I let my songs pile up only to share them with a few friends. This year I’ve decided to share them with the world. I open myself up to all kinds of opinions — it’s taken a little courage. Of course, there are nice people too, and that makes it worth all the trouble.

Purse Thief
Sounds like: Poetry-laced indie rock from New Mexico that pays homage to Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers with a sound that will certainly appeal to fans of Viagra Boys.
Interview:
Describe your approach to music and how you would explain your sound to others.
The approach is, try to make the thing you wanna hear in the world not make the thing you’ve heard. Be a good listener, a good performer, take what you’ve learned and try and make it yours, make it fun. The resistance can be a good time. We sound like old rocknroll got in a car chase with some punk rockers from New Mexico.
How did you come up with the name of your act?
Purse Thief was a way of taking a descriptor/stereotype applied to criminals and minorities and turning it on its head. Saying “the purse” is actually what’s been stolen from the people. Trying to incorporate this ethos of those who have given back to the poor. Taking a name that would possibly sound juvenile and adding an element of art and poetry to it, making people look twice.
What are some artists and albums that have informed your creative direction?
I think we are all a bit all over the map: The Velvet Underground (Banana Album) At the Drive-In (Relationship of Command) The Dead Boys, Patti Smith, Dylan, John Prine, Lee Moses, The Sex Pistols, The Refused, early 90’s hip-hop. Anyone who could fit a message inside some good poetry and still have it feel straight-foward.
What’s the most exciting thing happening in music right now?
I think the resurgence of a DIY scene, underground venues popping up again. Seeing what the knee’-jerk reaction is musically to this chaotic state of corruption and decline. I love the Australian Punk Scene and some of the stuff coming out of the small towns again. Feeling like people are crying out for good music again, that desperation being answered.
Where do you see the music world heading in the next five years?
In this moment, we are seeing humans beg other humans to support human made art and human made music, the logical place of where that leads is another chasm, another culture war, more fragmentation, it takes about 25 minutes of uninterupted time to regain your concentration from distractions. we might be dealing with humans who will never know what that’s like, to have that. I think more than ever putting on a record will be a form of meditation, real raw live music will have this feeling of something dangerous again. I don’t know where it heads but I know we need good artists more than ever.
How is music helping you during these uncertain times?
It’s giving me something to write about that’s for sure, music makes fast friends of us, watching a song travel the world is one of those journeys that feels like a deep adventure. When you find something you wanna put on repeat, that’s love.
The Difference Machine

Our approach is based on feeling. Music is to be felt first and foremost. The technical stuff is all based around that. We sculpt our decisions in service to the feeling. Something that took us a considerable amount of time to figure out. Sometimes feelings are difficult to sort through. We have to connect spirit with our humanity. I honestly wouldn’t explain our sound to others. That’s for them to figure out…what it means to them. We just present what we have. Art is subjective, and however they interpret is cool with us.
How did you come up with the name of your act?
That’s a funny one lol. A lot of bad names were thought of before we arrived at TDM. I can’t remember the exact origin. I know it was a combo of conspiracy and Brannon Boyle’s brainchild (our ‘manager’ and booking agent)
What are some artists and albums that have informed your creative direction?
Our influences run the gamut. From 13th Floor Elevators to Outkast to Zappa to Dilla to edan to Company Flow to Brian Jonestown to Marvin Gaye and George Clinton to Sun Ra. We are the children of them all. And so so, so many more.
What’s the most exciting thing happening in music right now?
I couldn’t pinpoint it to one specific thing. I think we’re most inspired by the people around us. The ones who don’t have millions of views or streams but are just as, if not more, talented. Where do you see the music world heading in the next five years?
Hmmm… I’m not sure. And I’m not sure it matters. We keep the pedal to the floor regardless of what’s going on around us. In all times, Creators must create.
How is music helping you during these uncertain times?
In our eyes, times are always uncertain. As soon as anyone thinks things are all good, boom, something crazy happens.
